  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and Practical
<br class="ltx_break">Multilingual Translation Models in the Wild</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Tencent Hunyuan Team
</span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Hy-MT3 is the third generation of the Hunyuan multilingual translation model family, including <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-MT3-1.8B</span>, <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-MT3-7B</span> and <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (MoE)</span>. Compared with Hy-MT2, Hy-MT3 translates <span id="abstract1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">more accurately, more completely and more faithfully to user constraints</span>: on real-world scenario data, the share of samples with mistranslations is reduced by <span id="abstract1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">43%</span>, omissions or additions by <span id="abstract1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">74%</span>, and instruction-following errors by <span id="abstract1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">40%</span>, while language coverage is expanded from <span id="abstract1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">38 to 102</span> languages.
With only 3B activated parameters, <span id="abstract1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models in non-thinking mode</span>, including flagship models such as Qwen3.8-Max, Kimi-K3.1-Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and approaches the strongest closed-source thinking models such as GPT-6.1-Sol and Gemini-4-Argon, while surpassing models that consume <span id="abstract1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">more than 30<math id="abstract1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math></span> its inference compute.
Beyond general translation, Hy-MT3 is optimized for two industrial scenarios. For <span id="abstract1.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">game localization</span>, built with high-quality game-domain data and a professional evaluation system from the Honor of Kings team, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B matches or outperforms strong closed-source models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro on all core metrics, and can be plugged into game development pipelines through the open-source toolchain TiMiHOKGameTranslator. For <span id="abstract1.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">image translation</span>, Hy-MT3 improves context understanding and error correction to better tolerate OCR errors, achieving the best result among models of comparable size.
Finally, we open-source <span id="abstract1.1.13" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TransRubric</span>, a rubric-based automatic evaluation suite for translation, which outperforms other evaluation schemes on the WMT26 metrics shared task test set and is more stable with respect to human evaluation.</p>
    
<p id="abstract1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-2.0pt;"><img src="2611.27673v2/logo/hugging.png" id="abstract1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:16/16;" width="16" height="16" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span> <a href="https://huggingface.co/collections/tencent/hy-mt3" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/collections/tencent/hy-mt3</a></p>
    
<p id="abstract1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="position:relative; bottom:-2.0pt;"><img src="2611.27673v2/logo/github.png" id="abstract1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:16/16;" width="16" height="16" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span> <a href="https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-MT3" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-MT3</a></p>
  
</div>

</div>

<figure id="S0.F1" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">

(T) denotes thinking mode; all other models, including Hy-MT3, are run in non-thinking mode.</figcaption>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>From Hy-MT2 to Hy-MT3</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building on Hy-MT1.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Hy-MT2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2026</a>)</cite> introduced a family of fast-thinking translation models (1.8B, 7B and 30B-A3B) for real-world translation that follow translation instructions in multiple languages. As Hy-MT2 was adopted by the open-source community and in more production scenarios, several limitations became apparent.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">First, <span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">faithfulness remains the main source of errors in real-world translation</span>. A fine-grained analysis of Hy-MT2-30B-A3B on 5,000 samples of real-world scenario data (Table <a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 3.5 Improvements over Hy-MT2 ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>) shows that 56.0% of its outputs contain at least one accuracy issue and 21.2% contain omissions or additions. Such errors are rarely captured by surface-level fluency, but they directly determine whether a translation can be used without post-editing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Second, <span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">language coverage is insufficient for long-tail demand</span>. Hy-MT2 covers 38 languages and performs poorly on lower-resource languages outside this set: on 64 additional lower-resource languages paired with Chinese or English, Hy-MT2-30B-A3B obtains a TransRubric score of only 63.89 (ZH<math id="S1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX) and 67.75 (EN<math id="S1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Third, <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">vertical scenarios impose requirements that general benchmarks do not measure</span>. Game localization requires strict preservation of placeholders and rich-text tags as well as consistent use of in-game terminology, and a single off-target or broken tag can break the game client. Image translation takes OCR output as input, which often contains misrecognized characters, missing text or wrong segmentation that the translation model must tolerate and correct from context.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">reliable automatic evaluation becomes the bottleneck</span>. As strong models converge on standard benchmarks, holistic scores and neural metrics <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guerreiro et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rei et al., 2022</a>)</cite> struggle to distinguish them or to explain where they fail. We need an evaluation method that is fine-grained, interpretable and consistent with human judgments, both to measure progress and to guide model development.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To address these issues, we present Hy-MT3. Our main contributions are as follows:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.5em;">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">More accurate, complete and constraint-faithful translation.</span> Compared with Hy-MT2-30B-A3B, the share of samples with mistranslations, omissions/additions and instruction-following errors is reduced by 43%, 74% and 40%, respectively, and language coverage is expanded from 38 to 102 languages (Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Supported Languages ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Outperforming much larger models with high efficiency.</span> Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated models in non-thinking mode, including Qwen3.8-Max, Kimi-K3.1-Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, and approaches the strongest closed-source thinking models such as GPT-6.1-Sol and Gemini-4-Argon.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Game translation.</span> Together with the Honor of Kings team, we improve game translation with high-quality game-domain data and a professional evaluation system. Hy-MT3-30B-A3B matches or outperforms strong closed-source models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro on all core metrics, and an open-source toolchain allows it to be integrated into game development pipelines for high-quality, low-cost localization.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Image translation.</span> Hy-MT3 is optimized for OCR-cascaded image translation, with stronger context understanding and error correction to tolerate OCR errors, achieving the best result among models of comparable size.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TransRubric.</span> We open-source TransRubric, an automatic evaluation suite for translation, which outperforms other evaluation schemes on the WMT26 metrics shared task test set and is more stable with respect to human evaluation.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>TransRubric: Rubric-Based Automatic Evaluation for Translation</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate translation quality in a fine-grained and interpretable way, we develop TransRubric, a rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kocmi &amp; Federmann, 2023</a>)</cite> evaluation suite, and use it as the primary metric throughout this report. Given a source text, a candidate translation, the translation instruction and optionally a reference translation, a TransRubric judge checks the candidate against a translation rubric, identifies each issue together with its error type (e.g., completeness, accuracy, terminology and instruction following) and severity level, in the spirit of MQM-style error annotation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lommel et al., 2014</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Freitag et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, and outputs a pointwise score on a 0–100 scale. The issue annotations make the score interpretable and enable error analyses such as Table <a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 3.5 Improvements over Hy-MT2 ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. TransRubric supports both reference-based evaluation (used for FLORES-200, WMT26, Mandarin<math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority and HardMTBench) and reference-free evaluation (used for WildMTBench-202611, which has no reference translations).</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In this report, each TransRubric score is the arithmetic mean of two judges, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2026</a>)</cite> and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026a</a>)</cite>. To make scores comparable across models, each benchmark score is computed with the fixed expected number of samples as the denominator, so empty outputs and unscored samples count as 0.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Meta-evaluation on WMT26.</span> We validate TransRubric on Task 2 (segment-level quality score prediction) of the WMT26 shared task on automated translation quality evaluation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lavie et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, following its official meta-evaluation on the eight priority translation directions: screen-based Pairwise Difference Pearson (PDP) at the segment level, source-based Soft Pairwise Accuracy (SPA) at the system level, and their average (Avg Corr). In this experiment, TransRubric runs reference-free with Gemini 3.6 Flash as the underlying judge. As shown in Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2 TransRubric: Rubric-Based Automatic Evaluation for Translation ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, TransRubric achieves the highest PDP (0.744) and Avg Corr (0.832), ahead of the top-ranked official submission Gemini-3.6-Flash (0.736 / 0.830), which uses the same underlying model, as well as GPT-5.6 Sol (0.828) and the ensemble system bytepop_pro10 (0.826). Its system-level SPA (0.920) is on par with the best system (0.924), and all LLM-based evaluators clearly outperform conventional metrics such as chrF, COMET22 and xCOMET.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Meta-evaluation on Task 2 (segment-level quality score prediction) of the WMT26 shared task on automated translation quality evaluation.</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<td id="S2.T1.2.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">COMET22</td>

<td id="S2.T1.2.7.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">0.862</td>
<td id="S2.T1.2.7.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">0.736</td></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.2.8" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S2.T1.2.12.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">0.426</td>

</table></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S2.T1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:338.1pt;"><span id="S2.T1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notes.</span> Results of all systems other than TransRubric are taken from Table 8 of the WMT26 findings <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lavie et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, which covers the eight priority translation directions. PDP is the screen-based Pairwise Difference Pearson at the segment level, SPA is the source-based Soft Pairwise Accuracy at the system level, and Avg Corr is their arithmetic mean; both are averaged equally across directions. <sup id="S2.T1.3.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S2.T1.3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup> marks reference-free evaluators and <sup id="S2.T1.3.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S2.T1.3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">†</span></sup> fine-tuned systems. The best result in each column is highlighted with an <span id="S2.T1.3.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFE6CC;">orange background</span>.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Comparison with human annotators.</span> We further compare TransRubric with 10 professional annotators majoring in English on 651 translations, i.e., 217 source texts with three candidate translations each, covering both Chinese<math id="S2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>English and English<math id="S2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Chinese. Each annotator scores every translation once on a 0–100 scale, and TransRubric (with the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B judges) scores every translation 10 times. Figure <a href="#S2.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 2 TransRubric: Rubric-Based Automatic Evaluation for Translation ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes the results.</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.5em;">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stability.</span> For each translation, we compute the standard deviation of its 10 scores. Across the 10 human annotators, the per-sample standard deviation averages 15.57 points, whereas across the 10 TransRubric runs it averages only 3.31 points (average variance 285.79 vs. 26.20). TransRubric scores are thus far more consistent than human judgments.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Pairwise accuracy.</span> For the three translations of each source text, we form all pairs (651 pairs in total) and check whether each rater prefers the same translation as the gold standard. The gold score of each translation is obtained by English translation experts, who revise the 10 annotators’ scores and take the average of the revised scores. Since the gold standard is built on the annotators’ own scores, this comparison may favor the human annotators. TransRubric reaches 59.91%, ranking 4th among the 11 raters: it is higher than 7 of the 10 annotators and lower only than three of them (61.29%, 60.37% and 60.06%), well above the human average of 54.7%.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2611.27673v2/transrubric_vs_human.svg" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/184;" width="476" height="184"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>TransRubric versus 10 human annotators on 651 Chinese<math id="S2.F2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>English translations. (a) Distribution of the per-sample standard deviation of the 10 scores, across annotators for humans and across 10 repeated runs for TransRubric; diamonds mark the means. (b) Pairwise accuracy of each rater; the dashed line marks the average of the 10 annotators.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">TransRubric is released together with Hy-MT3 at <a href="https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-MT3" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-MT3</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benchmarks.</span> We evaluate Hy-MT3 from three perspectives.</p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize" style="--ltx-enum-leftmargin:1.5em;">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">General translation.</span> FLORES-200 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Team et al., 2022</a>)</cite> on 33 languages with all <math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="33\times 32=1056" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>33</mn><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1056</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">33\times 32=1056</annotation></semantics></math> directions; FLORES-200 on 64 additional lower-resource languages paired with Chinese or English (256 directions); WMT26 GenMT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kocmi et al., 2026</a>)</cite> on 20 language pairs after excluding English<math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Ligurian, English<math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Ladin and English<math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Northern Sami; and Mandarin<math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority translation between Mandarin and Tibetan, Uyghur, Traditional Mongolian, Arabic-script Kazakh and Cantonese (10 directions).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Real-world translation.</span> WildMTBench-202611, the latest version of our in-the-wild benchmark, consists of 5,000 samples of real-world scenario data evenly distributed over 10 domains; HardMTBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2026b</a>)</cite> is an open-source benchmark of knowledge-intensive, long-form Chinese--English cases in both directions<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                    <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                    
                    
                    
                  <a href="https://github.com/jasonNLP/HardMTBench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/jasonNLP/HardMTBench</a></span></span></span>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Translation instruction following.</span> IFMTBench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2026</a>)</cite><span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                    <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                    
                    
                    
                  <a href="https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-MT2/tree/main/IFMTBench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hy-MT2/tree/main/IFMTBench</a></span></span></span> contains 7,344 samples covering industrial translation constraints such as code tags, inline code, layout preservation, style, glossary, context and structured data, split into single-constraint (Simple) and multi-constraint (Complex) subsets.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">In addition, we report human evaluation on game translation (Section <a href="#S3.SS7" title="3.7 Game Translation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.7</span></a>) and cascaded image translation on VISTA-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lv et al., 2026</a>)</cite> (Section <a href="#S3.SS8" title="3.8 Image Translation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.8</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Metrics.</span> We report TransRubric (Section <a href="#S2" title="2 TransRubric: Rubric-Based Automatic Evaluation for Translation ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) as the primary metric, and GEMBA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kocmi &amp; Federmann, 2023</a>)</cite> with GPT-OSS-120B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite> (medium reasoning) as a complementary LLM-based metric. IFMTBench is scored with its official rules and LLM judge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Baselines.</span> We compare Hy-MT3 with Hy-MT2 and three groups of baselines: (1) general models in non-thinking mode, including Kimi-K3.1-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moonshot AI, 2026</a>)</cite>, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2026</a>)</cite>, the Qwen3.8 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026d</a>)</cite> / Qwen3.6 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2026b</a>)</cite> series and the Gemma4 series <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gemma Team, 2026</a>)</cite>; (2) translation-specialized models and commercial translation APIs, including the Index-Translate series <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2026a</a>)</cite>, Tower-Plus-72B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rei et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, Qwen-MT-Flash <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2025</a>)</cite>, Microsoft Translator, Volcano Translator and iFlytek Translator; and (3) models in thinking mode, including GPT-6.1-Sol <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2026</a>)</cite>, Claude-Opus-5.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2026</a>)</cite>, Gemini-4-Argon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google DeepMind, 2026</a>)</cite>, GLM-5.3 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">GLM-5 Team, 2026</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Z.ai, 2026</a>)</cite> and the thinking variants of the open-weight models above. All Hy-MT3 models are run in non-thinking mode, so the most direct comparison is with groups (1) and (2).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>General Translation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.2 General Translation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> reports results on general translation benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T2" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Performance comparison on general multilingual translation benchmarks.</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<div id="S3.T2.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:234pt;vertical-align:-115.8pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-183.8pt,124.7pt) scale(0.484205528134754,0.484205528134754) ;">
<table id="S3.T2.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.T2.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.9pt 4.0pt;" rowspan="2"><span id="S3.T2.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Models</span></td>

</table>
</span></div></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.T2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:338.1pt;"><span id="S3.T2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notes.</span> Each cell reports TransRubric / GEMBA scores on a 0–100 scale; higher is better. Both are reference-based LLM-as-a-judge metrics. TransRubric is the arithmetic mean of two pointwise judges, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, with scores averaged over the fixed expected number of samples. GEMBA uses GPT-OSS-120B with medium reasoning and is macro-averaged over language pairs. For both metrics, empty translations receive a score of 0.
For the 33-language FLORES-200 set, ZH<math id="S3.T2.m22" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX covers all directions involving Chinese, including Chinese–English; EN<math id="S3.T2.m23" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX covers directions involving English but not Chinese; and XX<math id="S3.T2.m24" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX covers directions involving neither Chinese nor English. <span id="S3.T2.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mand.<math id="S3.T2.m25" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Min.</span> denotes Mandarin<math id="S3.T2.m26" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority translation. <span id="S3.T2.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Avg.</span> is the unweighted mean of four benchmark-level scores: FLORES-200, FLORES-200 low-resource, WMT26 and Mand.<math id="S3.T2.m27" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Min.
<sup id="S3.T2.3.4" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.T2.3.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> denotes thinking mode; unmarked models use non-thinking mode. Our models are shown in bold. <span id="S3.T2.3.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFE6CC;">Orange</span> and <span id="S3.T2.3.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#CCFFFF;">blue</span> backgrounds indicate the best non-thinking and thinking results, respectively, in each metric column.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall result among all non-thinking systems.</span> Its average TransRubric / GEMBA scores reach 88.50 / 81.87, ahead of Qwen3.8-Max (88.02 / 81.08), Kimi-K3.1-Pro (86.01 / 81.47) and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (84.27 / 78.98). On the 33-language FLORES-200 set, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B obtains the best TransRubric scores among non-thinking systems on all three subsets (94.06 / 94.82 / 92.12 on ZH<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX, EN<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX and XX<math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Language expansion brings large gains on lower-resource languages.</span> On the 64 additional lower-resource languages, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B improves the TransRubric score over Hy-MT2-30B-A3B from 63.89 to 91.52 (ZH<math id="S3.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX), the best among non-thinking systems, and from 67.75 to 92.74 (EN<math id="S3.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX), close to Qwen3.8-Max (92.99). The gains are even larger for smaller models: Hy-MT3-1.8B improves from 24.44 to 73.48 on ZH<math id="S3.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>XX.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-MT3 is strong on WMT26 and Mandarin<math id="S3.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority translation.</span> On WMT26, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B improves over Hy-MT2-30B-A3B from 73.03 to 85.63 in TransRubric, close to the strongest non-thinking systems Qwen3.8-Max (86.88) and Kimi-K3.1-Pro (85.86). On Mandarin<math id="S3.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority translation, it achieves 83.85 / 70.17, the best among non-thinking systems on both metrics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Smaller models remain highly competitive.</span> Hy-MT3-7B reaches an average of 86.12 / 80.39, surpassing DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and all translation-specialized models, including Index-Translate-35B-A3B (78.75 / 79.24). Hy-MT3-1.8B improves the average TransRubric score of Hy-MT2-1.8B from 56.51 to 75.05, outperforming commercial APIs such as iFlytek Translator (73.26), Microsoft Translator (71.09) and Qwen-MT-Flash (67.00), as well as Index-Translate-2B (60.11).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2611.27673v2/fig_efficiency.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/272;" width="429" height="272"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>General translation quality versus inference compute. The x-axis is the estimated inference compute per test sample, approximately <math id="S3.F3.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="2\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2\times</annotation></semantics></math> activated parameters <math id="S3.F3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> generated tokens (including thinking tokens), in log scale. The y-axis is the average TransRubric score in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.2 General Translation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Arrows connect the non-thinking and thinking modes of the same model; dashed horizontal lines denote closed-source models whose sizes are undisclosed.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficiency.</span> Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.2 General Translation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> plots translation quality against estimated inference compute. Hy-MT3 models lie on the upper-left frontier: Hy-MT3-30B-A3B requires less than 1 TFLOP per sample, yet outperforms models that consume more than 30<math id="S3.SS2.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> its compute, such as Qwen3.8-Max and Kimi-K3.1-Pro in non-thinking mode. Thinking mode improves the quality of general models, but typically requires several times to more than an order of magnitude more compute.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">

</table>
</span></div></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.T3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:338.1pt;"><span id="S3.T3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notes.</span> All scores are on a 0–100 scale; higher is better. TransRubric follows the same two-judge protocol as in Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.2 General Translation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, with empty or missing outputs scored as 0. <span id="S3.T3.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">WildMTBench-202611</span> contains 5,000 real-world samples and reports reference-free TransRubric scores using the fixed expected number of samples as the denominator. <span id="S3.T3.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HardMTBench</span> contains bidirectional Chinese–English cases and reports TransRubric / GEMBA scores, with GEMBA macro-averaged over the two directions. <span id="S3.T3.3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">IFMTBench</span> is evaluated using its official rules and GPT-OSS-120B judge and reports the mean over valid samples. <span id="S3.T3.3.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Simple</span> and <span id="S3.T3.3.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Complex</span> denote the single- and multi-constraint subsets, respectively, and <span id="S3.T3.3.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Total</span> aggregates all 7,344 test cases across both subsets.
<sup id="S3.T3.3.8" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.T3.3.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> denotes thinking mode; unmarked models use non-thinking mode. A dash indicates that the model was not evaluated on the corresponding benchmark. Our models are shown in bold. <span id="S3.T3.3.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFE6CC;">Orange</span> and <span id="S3.T3.3.10" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#CCFFFF;">blue</span> backgrounds indicate the best non-thinking and thinking results, respectively, in each score column.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Real-world translation.</span> On WildMTBench-202611, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves 91.30, the best among non-thinking systems, ahead of Qwen3.8-Max (90.94) and Kimi-K3.1-Pro (90.23). It also outperforms several thinking models, such as Gemini-4-Argon<sup id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> (90.30) and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next<sup id="S3.SS3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> (90.40), and is close to GPT-6.1-Sol<sup id="S3.SS3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> (92.50). Notably, Hy-MT3-1.8B (84.45) already surpasses the previous-generation Hy-MT2-30B-A3B (83.62).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hard, knowledge-intensive translation.</span> On HardMTBench, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B improves over Hy-MT2-30B-A3B from 81.38 to 88.93 in TransRubric and clearly outperforms models of comparable size, such as Index-Translate-35B-A3B (85.57), Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (84.26) and Gemma4-26B-A4B (83.01). However, a gap remains compared with much larger models such as Qwen3.8-Max (92.30) and Kimi-K3.1-Pro (92.04). This suggests that in knowledge-intensive scenarios, larger models benefit from their greater parameter capacity to store world and domain knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Translation instruction following.</span> On IFMTBench, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves 91.02 / 79.74 / 86.66 on Simple, Complex and Total, obtaining the best Simple and Total scores among non-thinking systems and surpassing thinking models such as Qwen3.8-Max<sup id="S3.SS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> (86.32), DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash<sup id="S3.SS3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> (85.37) and Claude-Opus-5.5<sup id="S3.SS3.p4.1.4" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.SS3.p4.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> (82.82) in Total. On Complex instructions, it still trails Qwen3.8-Max (82.84) and Kimi-K3.1-Pro (82.21), indicating room for improvement under multi-constraint instructions. Hy-MT3-7B (83.66) also surpasses Hy-MT2-30B-A3B (83.35).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Domain-Wise Analysis</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further break down WildMTBench-202611 into 10 domains (Table <a href="#S3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 3.4 Domain-Wise Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S3.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Domain-Wise Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best score among non-thinking systems in 5 of the 10 domains (politics, finance, technology, medical and others) and is within 0.35 points of the best in legal, education, culture &amp; entertainment and life &amp; social. The largest margin appears in the “others” domain, where Hy-MT3-30B-A3B leads Qwen3.8-Max by 3.23 points (90.93 vs. 87.70), indicating strong robustness on long-tail inputs. The largest remaining gap is in sports (90.17 vs. 91.14 for Qwen3.8-Max).</p>
</div>

<p id="S3.T4.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:338.1pt;"><span id="S3.T4.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notes.</span> All scores are reference-free TransRubric scores on a 0–100 scale; higher is better. <span id="S3.T4.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">WildMTBench-202611</span> contains 5,000 samples evenly divided into 10 domains of 500 samples each. Each domain score is the mean of the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B judge scores, using 500 as the fixed denominator; empty or missing translations are assigned a score of 0. <span id="S3.T4.3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Avg.</span> is the score over all 5,000 samples and, because the domains are equally sized, is also the unweighted mean of the 10 domain scores. Judge-side failures are also scored as 0 (one case each for Hy-MT3-30B-A3B and Hy-MT3-7B, and two cases for Claude-Opus-5.5<sup id="S3.T4.3.4" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.T4.3.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup>).
<sup id="S3.T4.3.5" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.T4.3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> denotes thinking mode; unmarked models use non-thinking mode. Commercial translation APIs were not evaluated and are omitted. <span id="S3.T4.3.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFE6CC;">Orange</span> and <span id="S3.T4.3.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#CCFFFF;">blue</span> backgrounds indicate the best non-thinking and thinking results, respectively, in each column.</p></div></div>
</figure>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>Domain-wise TransRubric scores on WildMTBench-202611. Numbers in parentheses are the overall averages. (T) denotes thinking mode.</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Improvements over Hy-MT2</h3>

<td id="S3.T5.2.8.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.8.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1.13</span></td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.8.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><math id="S3.T5.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>1.01 (<math id="S3.T5.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>47%)</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T5.2.9" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T5.2.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;" colspan="4"><span id="S3.T5.2.9.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">(b) Error types (share of samples, <math id="S3.T5.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>)</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T5.2.10" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T5.2.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error type</span></td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.10.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.10.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-MT2-30B-A3B</span></td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.10.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.10.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hy-MT3-30B-A3B</span></td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.10.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.10.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Rel. change</span></td></tr>

<td id="S3.T5.2.11.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.11.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5.5%</span></td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.11.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><math id="S3.T5.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>74%</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T5.2.12" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S3.T5.2.12.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">56.0%</td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.12.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.12.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">31.8%</span></td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.12.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><math id="S3.T5.m17" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>43%</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T5.2.13" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T5.2.13.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">Terminology</td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.13.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">28.3%</td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.13.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.13.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">17.9%</span></td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.13.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><math id="S3.T5.m18" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>37%</td></tr>
<tr id="S3.T5.2.14" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T5.2.14.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">Instruction following</td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.14.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;">16.5%</td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.14.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><span id="S3.T5.2.14.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">9.8%</span></td>
<td id="S3.T5.2.14.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 5.0pt;"><math id="S3.T5.m19" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>40%</td></tr>
</table></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.T5.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:338.1pt;"><span id="S3.T5.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notes.</span> All statistics are computed over the 5,000 WildMTBench-202611 samples using TransRubric scores and issue annotations.
<math id="S3.T5.m20" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.T5.m21" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math> indicate that higher and lower values are better, respectively.
“pt” denotes an absolute change in percentage points, while values in parentheses denote relative changes from Hy-MT2-30B-A3B.
In (b), each value is the share of samples containing at least one issue of the corresponding type; issue types are not mutually exclusive.</p></div></div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score distribution.</span> Hy-MT3 raises the average score from 83.62 to 91.30 (+7.68). The share of samples scoring at least 90 increases from 46.1% to 70.9%, and the poor-translation rate (score below 60) drops from 7.4% to 2.2%. In a per-sample comparison, Hy-MT3 wins on 58.9% of the samples and loses on only 15.5%.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Error types.</span> The improvements mainly come from faithfulness (Figure <a href="#S3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 3.5 Improvements over Hy-MT2 ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). The share of samples with omissions or additions drops from 21.2% to 5.5% (<math id="S3.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>74%), mistranslations from 56.0% to 31.8% (<math id="S3.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>43%), terminology issues from 28.3% to 17.9% (<math id="S3.SS5.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>37%), and instruction-following issues from 16.5% to 9.8% (<math id="S3.SS5.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>40%). The reduction in instruction-following issues mainly comes from Hy-MT3 no longer completing or extending the source text on its own, and from better preservation of formats and tags.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2611.27673v2/error_reduction.svg" id="S3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/190;" width="405" height="190"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>Share of samples containing each error type on WildMTBench-202611, Hy-MT2-30B-A3B versus Hy-MT3-30B-A3B (Table <a href="#S3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 3.5 Improvements over Hy-MT2 ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>b). Labels above each pair give the relative reduction.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span>Case Study</h3>

<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 3.6 Case Study ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> compares Hy-MT2 and Hy-MT3 on representative cases of the three error types where Hy-MT3 improves the most.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Mistranslation.</span> Hy-MT2 misreads the person name “夏雨雨” as “summer rains” and over-interprets “动容” as “moved to tears”, while Hy-MT3 correctly transliterates the name and keeps the original meaning. In the marketing copy, Hy-MT2 adds embellishments that are not in the source (“卓越功效”, “完美”), whereas Hy-MT3 translates “powerful pairing” and “designed to support” faithfully.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS6.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Omission.</span> Hy-MT2 drops key information such as “Chippy Exhibition” and “硬核”, while Hy-MT3 preserves it (“对抗激烈的表演赛”, “Hardcore shots”) together with the inline tags.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS6.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS6.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Instruction following.</span> Hy-MT3 keeps the author list and journal name of a bibliographic reference in their original form, following the citation convention, while Hy-MT2 translates them. When asked for a colloquial translation, Hy-MT3 produces a more conversational rendering than the formal output of Hy-MT2.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F6" class="ltx_figure">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>Case study comparing Hy-MT2 and Hy-MT3.</figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.7 </span>Game Translation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Game localization places strict requirements on output format and terminology: placeholders and rich-text tags must be preserved exactly, in-game terms must be translated consistently, and any off-target output can directly break the game client. Together with the Honor of Kings team, we collected high-quality game-domain data to make Hy-MT3-30B-A3B a leading model for game translation. We also jointly built an evaluation system covering multiple game genres. The evaluation set is stratified by localization characteristics such as text length, rich text and placeholders, and includes long texts with high terminology density from MOBA and open-world games, to comprehensively test how well a model handles game context, terminology and complex text structures. Under this system, we establish four game-specific evaluation criteria: off-target rate, placeholder errors, rich-text errors and terminology errors.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 3.7 Game Translation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the lowest error rate on all four criteria (tied with Gemini 3.1 Pro on placeholder errors) and the highest total score in human evaluation, outperforming strong thinking models such as Gemini 3.1 Pro (88.7), GPT-5.5 (88.6) and DeepSeek-V4-Pro (88.3). In particular, its terminology error rate is 0.08%, compared with 0.54% for Gemini 3.1 Pro.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS7.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS7.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The Honor of Kings team has also open-sourced a game translation toolchain<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/Tencent/TiMiHOKGameTranslator" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/Tencent/TiMiHOKGameTranslator</a></span></span></span> that supports multiple translation platforms, multiple file formats, pluggable workflows and various code management methods. It seamlessly embeds Hy-MT3-30B-A3B into the game development pipeline, connecting translation with downstream engineering. After integration, localization requires no additional manual effort, providing a reusable reference solution for game localization.</p>
</div>

<td id="S3.T6.2.1.7.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 4.0pt;">0.81%</td>
<td id="S3.T6.2.1.7.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.9pt 4.0pt;">83.2</td></tr>
</table>
</span></div></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.T6.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:338.1pt;"><span id="S3.T6.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notes.</span> The evaluation set and the human evaluation protocol are jointly built with the Honor of Kings team. Off-target, placeholder, rich-text and terminology errors are reported as the percentage of samples containing the corresponding error; lower is better (<math id="S3.T6.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>). The total score is the overall human rating; higher is better (<math id="S3.T6.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>).
<sup id="S3.T6.3.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.T6.3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> denotes thinking mode. Our model is shown in bold and thinking models in <span id="S3.T6.3.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">blue</span>.
The best result in each column is highlighted with an <span id="S3.T6.3.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFE6CC;">orange background</span>.</p></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.8 </span>Image Translation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In image translation, text in an image is typically first recognized by an OCR engine and then translated. OCR output often contains misrecognized characters, missing text or wrong segmentation, so the translation model must infer the intended content from context. We optimize Hy-MT3 for this scenario by strengthening its context understanding and error correction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS8.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS8.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on VISTA-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lv et al., 2026</a>)</cite> in a cascaded setting with PaddleOCR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cui et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 3.8 Image Translation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves 45.73, the best among non-thinking and translation-specialized models, ahead of Gemma4-26B-A4B (45.46) and Index-Translate-35B-A3B (43.63), and also above the thinking model GLM-5.3<sup id="S3.SS8.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.SS8.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> (42.84).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T7" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 7: </span>Translation quality on VISTA-Bench (text track, PaddleOCR input).</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</table></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="S3.T7.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:196.7pt;"><span id="S3.T7.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notes.</span> All scores are on a 0–100 scale.
Test data and the judging protocol are taken from VISTA-Bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lv et al., 2026</a>)</cite>, a multilingual image translation benchmark covering 23 source languages and 10 everyday-use domains with image-specific rubrics.
We evaluate in a cascaded setting: text in each test image is first recognized by PaddleOCR, and the recognized text is then given to each model for translation, so no model has access to the image.
Following the official protocol, a text-only LLM judge checks each translation against the image-specific rubric without seeing the image or the reference translation; each atomic criterion is scored as fully met or unmet, criteria are weighted by importance (core / supporting / minor <math id="S3.T7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=3/2/1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>3</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=3/2/1</annotation></semantics></math>), and we report the translation-quality (T) dimension averaged over all 506 translation directions.
Because OCR errors (misrecognized, missing or wrongly segmented text) propagate to the translation input and cannot be recovered without the image, the absolute scores of all models are considerably lower than on text-only benchmarks; the scores are intended for relative comparison under identical OCR input.
<sup id="S3.T7.3.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.T7.3.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">T</span></sup> denotes thinking mode; models without the marker are run in non-thinking mode.
Our model is shown in bold at the top, followed by
<span id="S3.T7.3.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FF8000;">general models in non-thinking mode</span>,
<span id="S3.T7.3.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#BF0040;">translation-specialized models</span>, and
<span id="S3.T7.3.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">models in thinking mode</span>.
The best result among non-thinking-mode systems is highlighted with an <span id="S3.T7.3.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#FFE6CC;">orange background</span>,
and the best result among <span id="S3.T7.3.7" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">thinking-mode</span> models with a <span id="S3.T7.3.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#CCFFFF;">blue background</span>.</p></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS9" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.9 </span>Quantization</h3>

<div id="S3.SS9.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To support deployment under different resource budgets, we evaluate Hy-MT3 under several quantization settings: FP8, and the Q8, Q4_K_M and IQ2 formats of llama.cpp, ranging from 8-bit to 2-bit precision. Table <a href="#S3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 3.9 Quantization ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Hy-MT3: More Accurate, Robust and PracticalMultilingual Translation Models in the Wild" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> compares them with the BF16 models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS9.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS9.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS9.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">8-bit and 4-bit quantization is nearly lossless for the larger models.</span> For Hy-MT3-7B, FP8, Q8 and Q4_K_M stay within 0.6 points of BF16 on every benchmark; for Hy-MT3-30B-A3B, the gap is within 0.4 points, and some settings even score slightly higher than BF16.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS9.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS9.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS9.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2-bit quantization remains usable.</span> With IQ2, the scores of Hy-MT3-7B and Hy-MT3-30B-A3B drop by at most 1.95 and 2.53 points, respectively, with the largest drops on low-resource FLORES-200, WMT26 and Mandarin<math id="S3.SS9.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority translation. Hy-MT3-30B-A3B-IQ2 still outperforms the BF16 Hy-MT3-7B on all benchmarks except Mandarin<math id="S3.SS9.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority translation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS9.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS9.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS9.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">The smallest model is more sensitive to quantization.</span> For Hy-MT3-1.8B, Q8 stays within 0.6 points of BF16 except on IFMTBench (<math id="S3.SS9.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="-" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>−</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-</annotation></semantics></math>1.60), whereas FP8 and Q4_K_M lower scores by up to 3.25 and 2.55 points, respectively, mainly on low-resource FLORES-200, Mandarin<math id="S3.SS9.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority translation and IFMTBench. Its scores on WildMTBench-202611 and HardMTBench drop by less than 0.6 points under all settings.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T8" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 8: </span>Performance comparison of Hy-MT3 models under different quantization settings.</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<p id="S3.T8.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle" style="width:338.1pt;"><span id="S3.T8.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Notes.</span> All scores are on a 0–100 scale. Except for IFMTB, scores are TransRubric scores averaged over the DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B judges. All-33 covers all pairs among the 33 FLORES-200 languages, while Low-Res. covers low-resource languages paired with Chinese or English. Mand, WMTB, HMTB and IFMTB denote Mandarin<math id="S3.T8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Leftrightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">⇔</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Leftrightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>Minority translation, WildMTBench-202611, HardMTBench and IFMTBench, respectively. IFMTB is independently judged by GPT-OSS-120B.</p></div></div>

<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present Hy-MT3, a family of multilingual translation models comprising Hy-MT3-1.8B, Hy-MT3-7B and Hy-MT3-30B-A3B. Compared with Hy-MT2, Hy-MT3 substantially reduces mistranslations, omissions/additions and instruction-following errors, and expands language coverage from 38 to 102 languages. Running in non-thinking mode with only 3B activated parameters, Hy-MT3-30B-A3B achieves the best overall performance among all evaluated non-thinking models on general translation, real-world translation and translation instruction following, and approaches the strongest closed-source thinking models at a fraction of their inference compute. Hy-MT3 further delivers leading results in game localization and OCR-cascaded image translation. Together with the models, we release TransRubric to support fine-grained and reliable evaluation of translation quality. We hope Hy-MT3 and TransRubric will facilitate both research and real-world applications of machine translation.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
